editorial.headline: Porcelain Household Ware With Room for Full-Scale Investment
editorial.standfirst: KBLI 23931 covers porcelain tableware, containers, display pieces, and ornamental ceramics, with national PMA access open across all business scales.
editorial.body:
KBLI 23931 sits in the practical, material world of porcelain household goods. Its scope is not merely dinner plates and cups, although those are central examples. It also reaches the wider domestic porcelain cabinet: saucers, bowls, teapots, pitchers, spoons, ashtrays, toilet articles, jars, and similar products used for carrying or packaging goods. The same activity also covers porcelain display and ornamental ceramic goods, including figures, statues, flower vases, cigarette boxes, urns, and comparable decorative pieces. In plain terms, this is the manufacturing code for porcelain objects that move between household utility, packaging use, and interior display.

The boundary matters because this is still a manufacturing activity, not a broad licence for every porcelain object a factory might imagine. The record expressly leaves porcelain sanitary fittings outside the activity, so the centre of gravity here is household equipment, containers, and decorative porcelain. A founder choosing this classification should therefore be able to describe production in terms of porcelain ware for domestic, packaging, or ornamental use, rather than drifting into adjacent building or sanitary product lines. The phrase “seluruh” in the slim record also signals that the activity is being treated inclusively within its own described scope, but only within that scope.

On scale, the code is unusually straightforward: it is open to micro, small, medium, and large enterprises. That means the classification can serve a modest workshop making ornamental porcelain pieces as well as a larger manufacturing operation producing household tableware or porcelain containers. The scale choice does not change the basic character of the activity; it changes the business size at which the activity is registered. For a founder, the editorial point is simple but important: the code is not reserved only for industrial-scale producers, nor is it confined to cottage production. It is written to accommodate the full span of Indonesian business scales listed in the record.

The national-versus-Bali picture is also clear. Nationally, the PMA status is open, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, based on the cited presidential regulation source in the record. Bali does not block PMA registration for this activity under the moratorium rule because the Bali-side risk note says that at large scale the OSS risk is medium-high or high, and therefore it is not caught by the provincial block on low and medium-low risk KBLI for PMA. The honest conclusion is that this is genuinely available for foreign-owned registration in Bali on the facts provided: nationally open, no foreign-equity reduction shown, and not blocked by Bali’s moratorium rationale.
